citations.quote:
Fix a real parameter $a_R>0$ and let the temperature coordinate range over the open interval $T\in(0,\infty)$. Define the entropy-only radiation state maps

$$\varepsilon_T(T):=a_RT^4,\qquad p_T(T):=\frac13a_RT^4,\qquad s_T(T):=\frac43a_RT^3.$$

Here $\varepsilon_T$ and $p_T$ are scalar-valued maps on $(0,\infty)$, and $s_T$ is the entropy coordinate as a scalar-valued map on the same interval. Put $h_T(T):=\varepsilon_T(T)+p_T(T)$. No particle-number coordinate, particle-number current, or chemical-potential coordinate is part of this state space.

Also define maps on the positive entropy-coordinate interval by

$$\tau(s):=\left(\frac{3s}{4a_R}\right)^{1/3},\qquad \varepsilon_s(s):=a_R\tau(s)^4,\qquad p_s(s):=\frac13\varepsilon_s(s),\qquad s\in(0,\infty).$$

The displayed formulas define functions on the stated domains. In the conventional SI physical reading, $T$ is measured in K, $a_R$ in J m$^{-3}$ K$^{-4}$, $\varepsilon_T,p_T$ in J m$^{-3}$, and $s_T$ in J m$^{-3}$ K$^{-1}$. These units do not assign an empirical value to $a_R$. In particular, this definition does not derive a quantum blackbody coefficient or assert that any physical system realizes these maps.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

Assume countable choice. Let $m\ge1$, let $U:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^m$, and let $A_1,A_2,A_3,B,M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be constant matrices. Assume $M=M^{\mathsf T}$ is positive definite, each $MA_j$ is symmetric, and $S:=(MB+B^{\mathsf T}M)/2$ is positive semidefinite. Consider

$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^3A_j\partial_{x_j}U+BU=0.$$

Use [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]: for $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ and multi-indices $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N^3$, the scalar seminorm is $p_{\alpha\beta}(f):=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^3}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$, and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$ consists of functions for which all these seminorms are finite. Here $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^m)$ means maps $U=(U_1,\ldots,U_m)$ with real-valued components such that each component, viewed as complex-valued with zero imaginary part, belongs to $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$; its vector seminorms are $p_{\alpha\beta}^{(m)}(U):=\max_{1\leq\ell\leq m}p_{\alpha\beta}(U_\ell)$. For $U_0\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^m)$ there is a unique global smooth solution, Schwartz in $x$ at each time and continuous in every $p_{\alpha\beta}^{(m)}$ on compact time intervals. With the negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform, put $\widehat U(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}U(x)\,dx$ and define, for $s\ge0$,

$$\|U\|_{H^s_M}^2:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}(1+|\xi|^2)^s\widehat U(\xi)^*M\widehat U(\xi)\,d\xi.$$

For $t\ge0$, $\|U(t)\|_{H^s_M}\le\|U_0\|_{H^s_M}$ for every $s\ge0$; hence the solution depends continuously on the data in each such norm. The same conclusions hold for smooth periodic data on the flat torus $\mathbb T_L^3:=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^3$, $L>0$, with Fourier coefficients $\widehat U_k=L^{-3}\int_{[0,L]^3}U(x)e^{-2\pi i k\cdot x/L}\,dx$ and

$$\|U\|_{H^s_M(\mathbb T_L^3)}^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k/L|^2)^s\widehat U_k^*M\widehat U_k.$$

For periodic data, $\|U(t)\|_\infty\le C_{s,L,M}\|U_0\|_{H^s_M(\mathbb T_L^3)}$ for each integer $s>3/2$.

For a unit vector $\nu\in\mathbb R^3$, write $A(\nu)=\sum_j\nu_jA_j$ and $\widetilde A(\nu)=M^{1/2}A(\nu)M^{-1/2}$. The finite speed

$$v_*:=\sup_{|\nu|=1}\max\{|\lambda|:\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(\widetilde A(\nu))\}$$

is finite. If $v_*>0$, $R>v_*t$, and $U_0$ vanishes on $B_R(x_0)$, then $U(t)$ vanishes on $B_{R-v_*t}(x_0)$ for $0\le t<R/v_*$. The same assertion holds on $\mathbb T_L^3$ using its geodesic distance. If $v_*=0$, every $A_j=0$ and the system is a pointwise linear ODE, so spatial support does not move. These are conclusions for the displayed linear systems; no variable-coefficient or nonlinear existence claim is included.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Differentiate the first system equation in time and take the divergence of the second. Substituting $\operatorname{div}q=-C\theta_t$ gives $C\tau\theta_{tt}+C\theta_t-\kappa\Delta\theta=0$, or $\tau\theta_{tt}+\theta_t-(\kappa/C)\Delta\theta=0$.

Expanding the derivative of $s_{\rm eff}$ and the divergence of $j_s$ gives $\partial_t s_{\rm eff}+\operatorname{div}j_s=\frac{C\theta_t+\operatorname{div}q}{T_0}-\frac{\theta(C\theta_t+\operatorname{div}q)+q\cdot(\tau q_t+\kappa\nabla\theta)/\kappa}{T_0^2}$. The first equation makes both occurrences of $C\theta_t+\operatorname{div}q$ zero, and the second gives $\tau q_t+\kappa\nabla\theta=-q$. Thus the expression equals $|q|^2/(\kappa T_0^2)$.

Differentiating $e_L$ and adding the flux divergence gives $\partial_t e_L+\operatorname{div}(\theta q)=\theta(C\theta_t+\operatorname{div}q)+q\cdot\left(\frac{\tau}{\kappa}q_t+\nabla\theta\right)=-\frac{|q|^2}{\kappa}$, where the first term vanishes by the energy equation and the second equality uses the Cattaneo equation. Since $C,\tau,\kappa>0$, $e_L$ is a positive definite quadratic form in $(\theta,q)$.

Write $U=(	heta,q)$, $e_j$ for the $j$th standard basis vector of $\mathbb R^3$, $A_j= egin{pmatrix}0&e_j^{\mathsf T}/C\(\kappa/	au)e_j&0_{3	imes3}\end{pmatrix}$, and $B=\operatorname{diag}(0,(1/	au)I_3)$. With $M=\operatorname{diag}(C,(	au/\kappa)I_3)$, $MA_j= egin{pmatrix}0&e_j^{\mathsf T}\e_j&0_{3	imes3}\end{pmatrix}$ is symmetric, $M$ is positive definite, and $S=(MB+B^{\mathsf T}M)/2=\operatorname{diag}(0,(1/\kappa)I_3)$ is positive semidefinite. For each unit $
u$, the longitudinal block of $A(
u)$ has eigenvalues solving $\lambda^2=\kappa/(C	au)$ and the two transverse eigenvalues are zero. Since $M$ is positive definite, $M^{1/2}$ is invertible and the supplier's matrix $M^{1/2}A(
u)M^{-1/2}$ is similar to $A(
u)$, so it has the same eigenvalues and maximum absolute eigenvalue $v_h=\sqrt{\kappa/(C	au)}$. Finally, $|	heta q\cdot
u|\le |	heta||q|\le 	frac12\sqrt{\kappa/(C	au)}(C	heta^2+(	au/\kappa)|q|^2)=v_h e_L$, since $2\sqrt{C	au/\kappa}|	heta||q|\le C	heta^2+(	au/\kappa)|q|^2$.

Fix a periodic solution from [F1]. For $k\ne0$, choose a coordinate $j$ with $|k_j|\ge |k|/\sqrt3$; periodic integration by parts $N$ times and $|\widehat{\partial_j^N U}_k|\le\sup_x|\partial_j^N U(t,x)|$ give $|\widehat U_k(t)|\le C_{N,t,L}(1+|k|)^{-N}$. For each integer $n\ge1$, the disjoint unit cubes centered at lattice points with $n\le|k|<n+1$ lie in an annulus of bounded extra width and volume $O((n+1)^2)$, so the shell has $O((n+1)^2)$ points. Hence $\sum_k(1+|k|)^{-N}<\infty$ for $N>3$, and the Fourier series converges absolutely and uniformly. To identify its sum with $U$, use the product Fejer kernel: in one dimension the normalized kernel is $F_N(y)=\frac1{L(N+1)}|\sum_{\ell=0}^N e^{2\pi i\ell y/L}|^2$. It is nonnegative with integral one, and for torus distance $|y|\ge\delta$ with $0<\delta<L/2$, the geometric-sum formula bounds it by $[L(N+1)\sin^2(\pi\delta/L)]^{-1}$. For the three-dimensional product, the mass outside the cube of coordinate distances less than $\delta$ is bounded by the sum of the three one-dimensional tail masses, hence tends to zero. Uniform continuity of $U(t,\cdot)$ then shows that convolution with these kernels converges uniformly to $U(t,\cdot)$. The convolutions are finite Fourier sums with weights $\prod_{j=1}^3(1-|k_j|/(N+1))_+$; absolute convergence makes the same sums converge uniformly to $\sum_k\widehat U_k(t)e^{2\pi i k\cdot x/L}$. Thus this series equals $U(t,x)$.

The matrices in step 1.4 have four components, positive-definite $M$, symmetric $MA_j$, and $S\ge0$, so they satisfy [F1]'s hypotheses under [A1]. The data class in the Statement is exactly the Schwartz/periodic class in [F1], using the componentwise Schwartz definition in [F2]. The eigenvalue computation in step 1.4 gives $v_*=v_h>0$. citations.quote:
Let $C,\kappa,\tau,T_0,L>0$. Let $\Omega$ be either $\mathbb R^3$ or the flat torus $\mathbb T_L^3:=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^3$, and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$. Consider real smooth fields $\theta:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ and $q:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ satisfying

$$C\theta_t+\operatorname{div}q=0,\qquad \tau q_t+q=-\kappa\nabla\theta.$$

The derivatives are ordinary derivatives of the Euclidean spatial coordinates; on the torus they are defined using periodic lifts. Write $U=(\theta,q)$ and let $e_j$ be the $j$th standard basis vector of $\mathbb R^3$. Define

$$A_j:=\begin{pmatrix}0&e_j^{\mathsf T}/C\\(\kappa/\tau)e_j&0_{3\times3}\end{pmatrix},\qquad B:=\operatorname{diag}(0,(1/\tau)I_3),\qquad M:=\operatorname{diag}(C,(\tau/\kappa)I_3).$$

Then the displayed system is $U_t+\sum_{j=1}^3A_j\partial_jU+BU=0$. The matrix $M$ is a positive symmetrizer, meaning $M=M^{\mathsf T}$ is positive definite and $MA_j$ is symmetric for each $j$. For a unit direction $\nu\in\mathbb R^3$, define the principal matrix $A(\nu):=\sum_{j=1}^3\nu_jA_j$; its eigenvalues are $0$ (multiplicity two) and $\pm v_h$, where $v_h:=\sqrt{\kappa/(C\tau)}>0$. For a fixed comparison speed $c_*>0$, $v_h\le c_*$ if and only if $\kappa\le C\tau c_*^2$.

For every such solution and every $s_0\in\mathbb R$, define the specified quadratic effective entropy density and flux by

$$s_{\rm eff}:=s_0+\frac{C\theta}{T_0}-\frac{C\theta^2}{2T_0^2}-\frac{\tau|q|^2}{2\kappa T_0^2},\qquad j_s:=\frac{q}{T_0}-\frac{\theta q}{T_0^2}.$$

Every smooth solution satisfies the exact identities

$$\partial_t s_{\rm eff}+\operatorname{div}j_s=\frac{|q|^2}{\kappa T_0^2}\ge0,\qquad \partial_t e_L+\operatorname{div}(\theta q)=-\frac{|q|^2}{\kappa},\qquad e_L:=\frac12\left(C\theta^2+\frac{\tau}{\kappa}|q|^2\right).$$

For every unit direction $\nu$, its quadratic flux satisfies $|\theta q\cdot\nu|\le v_h e_L$. The density $e_L$ is a positive quadratic Lyapunov density, not a physical energy density. The entropy identity asserts nonnegative production for this specified quadratic effective current; it does not assert positivity of $s_{\rm eff}$ for arbitrary data or a nonlinear material entropy law. These equations define the mathematical subsystem considered here; the sources give model context and do not establish a material-specific realization.

Use the exact global-solution, Fourier-coefficient, and weighted-norm conventions in [F1]. For initial data $U_0=(\theta_0,q_0)\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^4)$ or $C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^3;\mathbb R^4)$, the unique global smooth evolution, its weighted Sobolev contraction, and finite propagation at speed $v_h$ follow conditionally from [F1] after checking the matrices below. On $\mathbb T_L^3$, for every integer $r>3/2$, set

$$K_{r,L,C}:=C^{-1/2}\left(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k/L|^2)^{-r}\right)^{1/2}<\infty,$$

where $C>0$ is the heat-capacity coefficient and $\|\cdot\|_{H^r_M(\mathbb T_L^3)}$ is the norm in [F1]. The periodic global solution supplied conditionally by [F1] obeys $T_0+\theta(t,x)>0$ for all $t\ge0$ whenever $K_{r,L,C}\|U_0\|_{H^r_M(\mathbb T_L^3)}<T_0$. The constant uses only the temperature component $C|\widehat\theta_k|^2$ of the supplied quadratic norm, so it does not compare heat-flux and temperature coordinates by a least eigenvalue. Although [F1] states a generic periodic supremum bound with unspecified constant $C_{s,L,M}$, the explicit $K_{r,L,C}$ bound here is derived directly from Fourier reconstruction and the stated norm contraction.

If the symbols receive their conventional SI thermal interpretation, take $\theta,T_0$ in K, $C$ in J m$^{-3}$ K$^{-1}$, $\kappa$ in W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $\tau$ in s, $L$ in m, $q$ in W m$^{-2}$, and the comparison speed $c_*$ in m s$^{-1}$. Use the spatial coordinates in the inherited Fourier norms as their numerical values in metres, so the unit-frequency term in $1+|k/L|^2$ uses the reference length $1$ m. Then $s_0$ and $s_{\rm eff}$ have entropy-density units J m$^{-3}$ K$^{-1}$, $j_s$ has entropy-flux units J m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, and $e_L$ has units J K m$^{-3}$ rather than energy-density units. The norm $\|U\|_{H^r_M}$ has units $\sqrt{\mathrm{J\,K\,m^{-3}}}$ and $K_{r,L,C}$ has units $\sqrt{\mathrm{m^3\,K/J}}$, so their product has temperature units. These unit labels do not assert a physical realization of the linear subsystem.

derivations.claim: The strict inequality makes $\omega>0$, and $\phi(t)=\operatorname{Re}(\Theta e^{(-1/(2\tau)+i\omega)t})$ solves $\tau\phi''+\phi'+(\kappa k^2/C)\phi=0$, since $-1/(2\tau)\pm i\omega$ are the roots of $\tau\lambda^2+\lambda+\kappa k^2/C=0$.

Differentiating $q$ in $x_1$ gives $\operatorname{div}q=-C\phi'(t)\cos(kx_1)$, so $C\theta_t+\operatorname{div}q=0$. Also $\tau q_t+q=-\frac{C}{k}(\tau\phi''+\phi')\sin(kx_1)e_1=\kappa k\phi\sin(kx_1)e_1=-\kappa\nabla\theta$, where step 1.1 supplies the second equality and $\nabla\theta=-k\phi\sin(kx_1)e_1$. Thus both PDE hold.

The fields are smooth and periodic because $k=2\pi n/L$ and $\phi$ is smooth; $\Theta\ne0$ makes the mode nonzero. For $t\ge0$, $|\theta(t,x)|\le|\Theta|e^{-t/(2\tau)}<T_0$, so $T_0+\theta>0$. The mode's amplitude decays with the displayed exponential envelope. The entropy-production and Lyapunov identities are the exact identities of [F1], applied to this verified solution.
